questions.question: Did higher-quality holdouts generally score above lower-quality holdouts?
Did any clearly weak company receive an obviously strong SPS?
questions.evidence: Fab.com (Very Weak/Failed) scored lowest of all 5 (31.8), separated from the next-lowest (Rdio, 46.7) by 14.9 points.

questions.question: Did any clearly strong company receive an obviously weak SPS?
questions.evidence: Zenefits (Strong at-the-time) scored highest of all 5 (66.3).

questions.question: Did any business model systematically break the anchors?
questions.evidence: 5 distinct business models represented (DTC-pivot e-commerce, subscription streaming, services marketplace, delivery marketplace, freemium-SaaS-plus-commission), none producing a nonsensical or unrepresentable result. DoorDash and Rdio's low coverage (21.4% each) reflects the evidence density already present in these pre-built benchmark records, not an anchor failure -- no fresh research was performed for the holdouts (correctly: PASS C scores from existing frozen evidence only).

questions.question: Did missing public evidence create obviously misleading quality scores?
questions.evidence: DoorDash and Rdio, despite the lowest coverage, both land in the middle of the range on real, cited negative evidence (competitive crowding, a flat valuation step; a stark named-competitor scale gap) -- not falsely inflated or falsely crushed by the missingness itself.

questions.question: Did provisional anchors behave nonsensically?
questions.evidence: Homejoy's marketplace/services-labor-cost Unit Economics judgment landed sensibly (3, Weak) without forcing a family fit. Fab.com's qualitative Burn Efficiency (2) and Runway (3) tracked the severity of the evidence appropriately, not at either extreme.

questions.question: Did Customer Growth/Growth Velocity overlap materially distort a result?
questions.answer: NO -- did not have the opportunity to occur
questions.evidence: Neither dimension was simultaneously scoreable for any of the 5 holdouts (all blocked by evidence absence or, for Zenefits, the guidance-vs-actual discipline). The known limitation is real but was not exercised in this run.

questions.question: Did evidence concentration materially distort a pillar or SPS?
questions.answer: YES -- two real, significant new instances found, reported per instruction, not fixed
questions.evidence: See 'evidence_concentration_findings' below -- Zenefits' Product pillar (100% of its scored weight from one sentence) is the most concentrated single-pillar case found anywhere in this entire program.

questions.question: Did any dimension behave fundamentally differently from calibration?
questions.evidence: The neutral-5 default for genuine silence, the anti-bias-for-simple-products convention, and the projection-vs-actual growth-anchor discipline (re-exercised for Zenefits' 2014-actual/2015-guidance pair, consistent with the Etsy and Peloton precedents from the freeze sprint) all behaved identically to calibration.

questions.question: Did SPS compression materially prevent useful differentiation?
questions.evidence: Holdout SPS range is 31.8-66.3 (34.5 points), more than double the 15-company calibration range (50.9-67.0, 16.1 points). This reflects that this holdout set happens to include more evidentially extreme real-world cases (a severe multi-signal crisis; an extraordinary fundraising trajectory), not necessarily that the methodology's discriminating power changed -- but it demonstrates the methodology is NOT artificially compressed when the underlying evidence genuinely warrants separation.

evidence_concentration_findings.event: the single 'free, fast-to-deploy... relative to legacy brokers' sentence
evidence_concentration_findings.weight_concentration: 100% of Zenefits' scored Product pillar weight (.60 of .60 scored) traces to one short sentence -- the most concentrated single-pillar case found anywhere across this entire calibration program (exceeding Tesla's 55%-of-Financial-Health and Shopify's 100%-of-a-2-dimension-Traction-pillar cases).
evidence_concentration_findings.sps_impact: Product carries a .20 pillar weight -- a materially sized fraction of SPS resting on one fact, not three independently corroborated ones.
evidence_concentration_findings.classification: CALIBRATION IMPERFECTION, not structural failure -- this is the already-identified evidence-concentration phenomenon (Evidence Independence Metadata, specified but not yet implemented) manifesting in its most extreme form yet observed. Raises the implementation PRIORITY of EIM; does not indicate a new category of problem.

evidence_concentration_findings.weight_concentration: 100% of Fab.com's scored Financial Health weight (.55 of .55 scored) traces to one underlying event pattern -- the same event also informs Execution Track Record and Operational Execution in other pillars (cross-pillar spread there is legitimate; the Financial-Health-internal concentration is the concern).
evidence_concentration_findings.sps_impact: Financial Health carries only a .10 pillar weight -- smaller SPS exposure than Zenefits' Product case, but the within-pillar concentration ratio is identical (100%).
evidence_concentration_findings.classification: CALIBRATION IMPERFECTION -- same phenomenon, same not-yet-implemented remedy (EIM metadata), not a new or different problem.

calibration_imperfection_vs_structural_f: Both evidence-concentration findings above, and every other observation in this phase, are classified CALIBRATION IMPERFECTION. Nothing in this phase produced a finding that the pillar architecture, weight structure, missing-evidence rules, or aggregation formula themselves are wrong -- every result traces to evidence sparsity or to the already-known, already-specified (if not yet implemented) evidence-concentration pattern. No STRUCTURAL FAILURE is indicated by this phase.
